question: Under Pennsylvania's Statute of Frauds (33 P.S. Section 1), what form must a contract for the sale of real property take to be enforceable in court?
choice_a: No writing is required; a purely oral agreement is fully enforceable
choice_b: A signed writing identifying the parties and essential terms
choice_c: A writing witnessed by two notaries
choice_d: A recorded deed executed before any offer is accepted
explanation: 33 P.S. Section 1 requires conveyances of an interest in land, including contracts for the sale of real property, to be evidenced by a signed writing identifying the parties and essential terms in order to be enforceable -- a purely verbal real estate sale agreement is generally not enforceable in Pennsylvania.
source_note: 33 P.S. Section 1 (confirmed via research pass citing FindLaw's Pennsylvania statutory text and secondary legal-practice sources)

question: Under Pennsylvania's Statute of Frauds, a lease exceeding what length of term must also be in a signed writing to be enforceable?
explanation: 33 P.S. Section 1 extends the writing requirement to leases exceeding three years -- shorter-term leases may, in many circumstances, be created orally, but longer leases require a signed writing just like a sale contract.

question: In Kurland v. Stolker, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court addressed whether partial performance (such as making payments or taking possession) alone can overcome the Statute of Frauds' writing requirement. What did the Court hold?
choice_a: Any partial performance, however small, fully satisfies the Statute of Frauds
choice_b: Only full payment of the purchase price satisfies the writing requirement
choice_c: The Statute of Frauds does not apply once a buyer has taken possession
choice_d: Partial performance does not automatically save an otherwise-unenforceable oral real estate agreement
explanation: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court in Kurland v. Stolker held that actions like making payments or taking possession are, standing alone, insufficient to overcome the Statute of Frauds' writing requirement for a real estate agreement -- reinforcing the strength of the written-contract rule in Pennsylvania real property law.
source_note: Kurland v. Stolker (Pa.), cited via secondary legal-commentary sources discussing Pennsylvania's Statute of Frauds partial-performance doctrine; full case citation not independently pinpoint-verified against a primary case reporter in this research pass

question: Which type of deed offers the LEAST protection to a grantee among Pennsylvania's commonly used deed forms, because it contains no covenants of title?
explanation: A Pennsylvania quitclaim deed conveys whatever interest the grantor has, if any, without any covenants of title -- offering the least protection of the state's main deed forms, in contrast to general and special warranty deeds, which each provide some level of title guarantee.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated Pennsylvania real-estate-practice sources (deedclaim.com, mvsklaw.com) on the state's deed forms; not itself a pinpoint statutory citation, since deed covenant types are largely a matter of common-law and conveyancing custom rather than a single controlling statute

question: Which type of deed is generally considered the MOST commonly used deed form in Pennsylvania residential resale transactions, providing a limited warranty covering only the grantor's own period of ownership?
explanation: While the general warranty deed is often described as the 'gold standard' providing the broadest protection, secondary Pennsylvania conveyancing sources describe the special warranty deed -- which only guarantees against title defects arising during the grantor's own period of ownership -- as the more commonly used deed in everyday PA residential transactions.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated Pennsylvania real-estate-practice sources on customary deed usage; not independently pinpoint-verified against a single controlling statute, since deed form selection is largely a matter of private conveyancing custom rather than mandated by RELRA or the Pennsylvania Code

question: Under the Pearson VUE national broker content outline's contracts section, which of the following is listed as a required element of a valid contract?
choice_b: Recording with the county recorder of deeds
choice_c: Legally competent parties, lawful consideration, and a legal act/purpose, among other elements
choice_d: A minimum earnest money deposit of 10% of the purchase price
explanation: The national broker content outline's Section IV.B ('Required elements of a valid contract') lists voluntary agreement/promise, legally competent parties, lawful consideration, and legal act/purpose as the tested elements -- standard contract-law fundamentals rather than PA-specific statutory requirements.
source_note: Pearson VUE National/General Exam Content Outline for Brokers, effective April 1, 2025, Section IV.B (confirmed directly from the official candidate handbook PDF)

question: Which sales-contract disclosure, uniquely emphasized in Pennsylvania under RELRA Section 608.2(3), is NOT a standard requirement found in most other states' generic sales contract law?
choice_a: A statement disclosing the buyer's credit score
choice_b: A statement of the seller's marital status
choice_c: A statement of the broker's personal net worth
choice_d: A statement of the property's zoning classification (with a single-family-zoning exception), making the contract voidable by the buyer if omitted
explanation: RELRA Section 608.2(3)'s mandatory zoning-classification disclosure (with its buyer-side voidability remedy) is a distinctly Pennsylvania statutory requirement layered onto the sales contract, beyond the generic offer/acceptance/consideration framework tested nationally.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.608.2(3) (confirmed verbatim, cross-referenced from the Commission/Compensation bucket of this bank)

question: Under general contract law tested on the national portion of the broker exam, what is the difference between a 'void' and a 'voidable' contract?
choice_a: A void contract has no legal effect from the outset, while a voidable contract is valid and enforceable unless and until the party with the right to disaffirm elects to rescind it
choice_b: There is no legal difference between the two terms
choice_c: A voidable contract can never be enforced under any circumstances
choice_d: A void contract can be ratified by either party at any time
explanation: This is standard contract-law doctrine tested under the national outline's 'Contract performance' subtopic (executed vs. executory, valid vs. void, voidable vs. unenforceable): a void contract never had legal effect, while a voidable contract remains valid unless the party entitled to disaffirm it chooses to do so.
source_note: hedge: standard national contract-law doctrine tested under the Pearson VUE National/General Exam Content Outline for Brokers, Section IV.C ('Contract performance'); not a PA-specific statutory citation

question: What is 'equitable title,' as tested under the national broker content outline's sales-contract subtopics?
choice_a: The interest a seller retains after closing has occurred
choice_b: The interest a buyer holds under a fully executed purchase contract, before legal title actually transfers at closing
choice_c: A form of title insurance unique to condominium purchases
choice_d: The interest a lender holds under a promissory note
explanation: 'Equitable title' -- listed under the national outline's Section IV.D ('Sales contract') -- refers to the beneficial interest a buyer acquires upon execution of a valid, binding purchase contract, even though legal title does not pass to the buyer until the deed is delivered at settlement.
source_note: hedge: standard national contract-law/property doctrine tested under the Pearson VUE National/General Exam Content Outline for Brokers, Section IV.D; not a PA-specific statutory citation

question: Under RELRA Section 608.1(3), what must a broker-principal agreement disclose regarding the possibility of the broker representing more than one consumer in a single transaction?
choice_a: Nothing -- dual representation disclosure is purely optional in listing agreements
choice_b: Only that the broker will never represent more than one party, since Pennsylvania bans this practice
choice_c: A statement identifying that possibility and explaining the duties that may be owed to the other party, and whether the broker may accept a fee for those services
choice_d: A statement limited to disclosing the broker's office address
explanation: Section 608.1(3) requires the written agreement to flag the possibility of the broker (or any affiliated licensee) providing services to more than one consumer in the same transaction, explain the duties potentially owed to that other party, and disclose whether a fee may be accepted for those services -- tying agency disclosure directly into the contract-formation stage.

question: Under RELRA Section 609, how long does a purchaser have to cancel a time share or campground membership purchase contract, and can that right ever be waived?
choice_a: 72 hours, and the right may be waived if the purchaser signs a waiver form
choice_c: There is no statutory cancellation right for these purchases in Pennsylvania
choice_d: Until midnight of the fifth day following execution of the contract, and the right may NOT be waived by the purchaser
explanation: RELRA Section 609(a) gives the purchaser until midnight of the FIFTH day following execution of a time-share or campground membership purchase contract to cancel, and Section 609(e) expressly makes this right non-waivable by any purchaser, regardless of contract language.

question: Within how many business days after receiving a purchaser's notice of cancellation of a time share/campground membership purchase must all payments be refunded?
explanation: RELRA Section 609(d) requires all payments made under the purchase contract to be refunded within 10 business days after receipt of the cancellation notice, along with a written acknowledgment that the contract is void; any promotional prizes or gifts already given to the purchaser remain the purchaser's property even after cancellation.

question: A violation of RELRA Section 609's time-share/campground cancellation-right provisions constitutes a violation of which additional Pennsylvania consumer-protection statute?
choice_a: The Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law
choice_b: The Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law
choice_d: No additional statute is implicated -- RELRA is the exclusive remedy
explanation: RELRA Section 609(g) provides that a violation of the time-share/campground cancellation-right section is ALSO deemed a violation of the Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law (act of December 17, 1968, P.L.1224, No.387), giving the Attorney General independent enforcement authority alongside the Real Estate Commission's own authority under RELRA.

question: Under RELRA Section 610, how long does a consumer generally have to cancel a sales agreement for a 'wholesale transaction' that contains the statutorily required disclosure information?
choice_a: Until midnight of the 5th day after execution, matching the time-share cancellation period
choice_b: There is no cancellation right for wholesale transactions under any circumstance
choice_c: Until midnight of the 30th day after execution, or until conveyance, whichever occurs first
choice_d: 180 days after execution, regardless of conveyance
explanation: RELRA Section 610(a) gives a wholesale-transaction consumer 30 days to cancel a properly disclosed sales agreement (or until conveyance, if sooner); if the agreement OMITS the required Section 610(e) disclosures, the consumer may cancel at ANY time before conveyance, and this right is likewise non-waivable.

question: If a wholesale-transaction sales agreement does NOT contain the disclosure information required under RELRA Section 610(e), what is the consumer's cancellation right?
choice_a: The consumer loses all cancellation rights entirely
choice_b: The cancellation window shrinks to just 24 hours
choice_c: The agreement becomes automatically void with no consumer action needed
choice_d: The consumer may cancel the agreement at any time prior to conveyance
explanation: RELRA Section 610(a) specifically extends the cancellation window indefinitely (up until conveyance) when the required Section 610(e) disclosures are missing from the sales agreement -- an incentive for wholesalers to include the mandated disclosures rather than face an open-ended cancellation exposure.

question: Does RELRA Section 609's time-share/campground cancellation right override or reduce a purchaser's separate rights under Pennsylvania's condominium law (68 Pa.C.S. Part II, Subpart B)?
choice_a: No -- Section 609(i) states nothing in the act affects rights conferred on the purchaser under the condominium law
choice_b: Yes -- Section 609 fully preempts and replaces any condominium-law purchaser rights
choice_c: Condominium law and RELRA are mutually exclusive and can never both apply to the same purchase
choice_d: This interaction has never been addressed in Pennsylvania statute
explanation: RELRA Section 609(i) is a savings clause: it clarifies that nothing in the time-share/campground cancellation section diminishes any separate rights a purchaser has under Pennsylvania's Uniform Condominium Act (68 Pa.C.S. Part II, Subpart B) -- the two protections operate cumulatively, not as substitutes for one another.
